rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The commentary links vv. 17–18 with 6:54 and 16:119; doing evil includes general disbelief and particular disobedience.
rows.anchor: Doing evil here may include a general state of

rows.speaker: most commentators
rows.claim: Most commentators include deliberate sins committed without knowledge of their full consequences or the Divine punishment they entail.
rows.anchor: claiming that it refers to anyone who sins, even purposefully, while being ignorant of the full repercussions or Divine punishment

rows.speaker: most commentators
rows.claim: Another interpretation treats anyone disobeying God as effectively being in a state of ignorance.
rows.anchor: asserting that anyone who commits an act of disobedience to God is, effectively, in a state of ignorance

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph's fear in 12:33 and the woman identified as Zulaykhā in 12:89 illustrate intentional sin described as ignorance.
rows.anchor: where the woman who attempted to seduce Joseph, identified in Islamic tradition as Zulaykhā, is said to have been in a state of ignorance

rows.speaker: Some
rows.claim: Some argue the phrase must refer to intentional sins, since unintentional sins require no repentance.
rows.anchor: Some even argue that it must refer to sins committed intentionally, since unintentional sins do not require repentance at all

rows.speaker: Some; others; still others
rows.claim: Views differ on when repentance is quick enough: during health, before death is certain, or any time before death.
rows.anchor: Some say repentance must occur while one is still in a state of health; others, that it must be prior to the certainty of death

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A hadith saying repentance remains open until the sun rises in the West supports a broader time frame.
rows.anchor: The broadening of the time frame seems justified by a ḥadīth that states, “The door of repentance is open until the sun rises from the West”

rows.speaker: God
rows.claim: A sacred hadith likewise says God does not bar Adam's repentance while his spirit remains in him.
rows.anchor: in the first person

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because true repentance requires amends and resolve not to return, one should repent while mentally lucid, physically able, and morally responsible.
rows.anchor: true repentance requires making amends and demonstrating that one will not return to the sinful behavior, one should repent while one is still in a state of mental lucidity, physical capability, and moral responsibility

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If repentance is not quick, the sinner may hope for forgiveness but cannot count on it with certainty, as linked to 9:102.
rows.anchor: the sinner can still hope for forgiveness from God (cf. 9:102), but cannot count on it with certainty

rows.speaker: Most
rows.claim: Most hold that true repentance requires abstaining from the particular sin in the future.
rows.anchor: Most hold that true repentance requires abstaining from that particular sin in the future

rows.speaker: Muʿtazilites
rows.claim: Muʿtazilites instead require abstaining from sin in general thereafter.
rows.anchor: Muʿtazilites, one of the two major schools of Sunni theology, held that it required abstaining from sin in general thereafter

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God is not obligated to accept repentance by human action; He has promised to do so and is true to His promise.
rows.anchor: It is not correct to say that God is obligated to accept repentance under these conditions, but rather that He has promised to do so in myriad verses and He is true to His Promise

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If God is called obligated to forgive, the obligation is self-imposed, not a response to human action, as 6:12 says He prescribed Mercy for Himself.
rows.anchor: If He can be described as “obligated” to forgive, He is obligated only by Himself

rows.speaker: Some
rows.claim: Some hold that vv. 17–18 were abrogated by 4:48 and 4:116, which leave sins other than idolatry open to forgiveness.
rows.anchor: Some maintain that this verse was abrogated by vv. 48 and 116, in which all sins other than idolatry are open to the possibility of Divine Forgiveness

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Repenting from a major sin does not necessarily avert its prescribed worldly punishment.
rows.anchor: Repentance of a major sin does not necessarily avert the worldly punishment prescribed for it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Anʿām is Makkan and addresses the Prophet and Muslims' struggle with Makkan idolatry; its central aim is to refute idolatry and invented ritual practices.
rows.anchor: al-Anʿām clearly addresses the challenges faced by the Prophet and the Muslims engaged in a religious struggle with the idolatrous Makkans

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah's name comes from Makkan cattle prohibitions; the Quran rejects these restrictions as human inventions and says God permits the cattle He created for consumption.
rows.anchor: The sūrah takes its name from the discussion of idolatrous ritual prohibitions on the consumption of certain kinds of cattle

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah refutes worship of idols, celestial bodies, and jinn, and challenges the Makkans' invented religious practices.
rows.anchor: The primary concern of the sūrah is to refute through powerful arguments various kinds of idolatry in general—including the worship of idols, celestial bodies, and jinn

rows.speaker: Many
rows.claim: Many regard it as a late Makkan surah, reflecting the Prophet's final effort to persuade the Makkans before his 622 migration to Madinah.
rows.anchor: Many consider this sūrah to be a late Makkan one and thus to reflect the culmination of the Prophet’s struggle and effort to persuade the Makkans

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet is addressed throughout and given arguments and challenges for disbelievers; the surah sums up the Quranic case against idolatry.
rows.anchor: The Prophet is directly addressed throughout the sūrah and given specific arguments and challenges to pose to the disbelievers in Makkah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A hadith reports that al-Anʿām descended all at once with seventy thousand angels praising and glorifying God.
rows.anchor: According to a ḥadīth, “Sūrat al-Anʿām was sent down all at once, accompanied by seventy thousand angels, hymning glorifications and praises”

rows.speaker: al-Zamakhsharī
rows.claim: A longer version adds that the seventy thousand angels seek forgiveness for whoever recites al-Anʿām with each verse, day and night.
rows.anchor: A longer version of thisḥadīth cited by al-Zamakhsharī adds

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another report says 6:59 was sent down with twelve thousand angels of its own.
rows.anchor: Another report mentions that one particular verse

rows.speaker: Some early authorities
rows.claim: Some early authorities considered certain verses, possibly those listed, to have been revealed in Madinah.
rows.anchor: Some early authorities, however, considered certain verses, perhaps vv. 20, 23, 91, 93, 114, 141, and 151–53, to have been revealed in Madinah

rows.speaker: Some
rows.claim: Some place the revelation of 6:145, which names four forbidden meats, at the Farewell Pilgrimage on the Day of ʿArafah.
rows.anchor: Some consider v. 145, which designates four kinds of meat forbidden to Muslims, to have been revealed during the Farewell Pilgrimage on the Day of ʿArafah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 1–3 present God as the universal and omniscient Creator.
rows.anchor: The sūrah begins with a powerful statement of God as the universal and omniscient Creator (vv. 1–3)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 4–31 reject the Makkans' excuses and recall earlier peoples destroyed for ignoring messengers, previewing the rejecters' fate in the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: After rejecting the Makkans’ excuses for not heeding the warning of the Prophet Muhammad, the sūrah continues with a reminder of the fate that befell previous generations

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 32–36 console the Prophet over the Makkans' rejection.
rows.anchor: Vv. 32–36 seek to console the Prophet in the face of the Makkans’ rejection

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 37–73 present arguments and statements the Prophet is instructed to use in response to the idolaters' rejection of the Quranic message.
rows.anchor: vv. 37–73 include a series of arguments and statements

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 74–83 recount Abraham's case against worshipping other than God: celestial bodies are ephemeral and changing despite their people's belief in their power.
rows.anchor: he points out to his people that even the celestial bodies, which they considered to have great power over the earth and its inhabitants, were ephemeral and changing

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 84–92 mention prophets and revelations after Abraham and place the Quran within, and as confirmer of, that prophetic and scriptural legacy.
rows.anchor: concluding with a mention of the Quran as part of, and a confirmer of, this prophetic and scriptural legacy

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 95–99 discuss God as giver of life and death in this world and the next.
rows.anchor: Vv. 95–99 discuss God as the giver of both life and death, in this world and the next

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Later passages reject arbitrary Makkan meat prohibitions and child sacrifice, replacing them with simpler revealed dietary rules and the commands and prohibitions in 6:151–153.
rows.anchor: several verses in the latter half of the sūrah address the arbitrary restrictions on the consumption of certain kinds of meat as observed by the Makkan idolaters—along with the pre-Islamic Makkan practice of “slaying their children”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After further warnings, verses 161–164 conclude with monotheistic belief and devotion, which the Prophet is instructed to declare amid Makkan resistance.
rows.anchor: the sūrah concludes with a powerful statement of monotheistic belief and utter devotion to the One God that the Prophet is instructed to issue in the face of continuing Makkan resistance

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The final verse says God makes generations succeed one another and frames worldly vicissitudes as a test of human character.
rows.anchor: the final verse (v. 165) invokes the idea that God causes generations to succeed one another in the life of the world, whose vagaries are merely a test of individual human character
